title: Berkshire 2003 letter: owner-capitalism boards, float economics, and buying Clayton and McLane on trust
summary: Buffett's 2003 letter explains how Berkshire judges itself against the S&P, why it prefers whole businesses when stocks are pricey, and how it buys companies on character and trust. It also covers director independence through real ownership, insurance float, avoiding derivatives, and owning up to mistakes.

principles.text: Judge performance by per-share intrinsic value gains versus the S&P; otherwise you add nothing an index fund doesn't.
principles.quote: Unless we achieve gains in per-share intrinsic value in the future that outdo the S&P’s performance, Charlie and I will be adding nothing to what you can accomplish on your own.

principles.text: Buy businesses with enduring economics, talented and honest managers, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: (1) have favorable and enduring economic charac-teristics; (2) are run by talented and honest managers and (3) are available at a sensible price.

principles.text: Idle capital is painful, but far better than doing something stupid.
principles.quote: Our capital is underutilized now, but that will happen periodically. It’s a painful condition to be in – but not as painful as doing something stupid.

principles.text: True director independence comes from real ownership: directors should win and lose big alongside shareholders.
principles.quote: You win, they win big; you lose, they lose big. Our approach might be called owner-capitalism.

principles.text: In insurance, a copyable product means managerial brains, discipline and integrity are the moat; float is only good if cheap.
principles.quote: The critical variables, therefore, are managerial brains, discipline and integrity.

principles.text: Never reach for yield by loosening credit standards or extending maturities; take risk only when paid for it.
principles.quote: Charlie and I detest taking even small risks unless we feel we are being adequately compensated for doing so.
